such (first syllable often shortened), which Apollonius in On Syntax p. 110 observed is more common in ordinary usage than τοιόσδε. The oldest neuter form is τοιοῦτο, likewise τοσοῦτο, which Herodotus and the other Ionic writers used consistently, but the Attic writers preferred τοιοῦτον and τοσοῦτον to such an extent that very few examples are found among the dramatic poets whose meter requires τοιοῦτο and τοσοῦτο, while hundreds require τοιοῦτον or τοσοῦτον: as Elmsley observed on Aesch. Pr. 800, Soph. OR. 734, OC. 789 and Eur. Med. 254, and likewise prose writers preferred τοιοῦτον and τοσοῦτον, so that examples of the other form, whether written in full τοιοῦτο τοσοῦτο or with elision τοιοῦτ᾽ and τοσοῦτ᾽, seem to be attributable to scribes rather than authors. Of the few examples I mentioned, where the meter requires τοιοῦτο and τοσοῦτο or τοιοῦτ᾽ and τοσοῦτ᾽, the reading is not even sufficiently certain, since these forms could have been introduced by scribes for τοιόνδε τοσόνδε or τοιόνδ᾽ and τοσόνδ᾽, as in Aeschylus Pr. 801 τοιοῦτο μέν σοι τοῦτο φρούριον λέγω, where Elmsley corrected τοιοῦτον ἕν σοι, and Blomfield plausibly τοιόνδε μέν σοι. Cf. Thes. vol. 7 p. 2262. τοσοῦτο Eum. 201, 427, where the meter allows τοσοῦτον. The meaning of this adjective is the same as that of τοιόσδε, "such", often used with emphasis, but generally in a bad sense, as in the very first passage Pr. 28 τοιαῦτ᾽ ἐπηύρου τοῦ φιλανθρώπου τρόπου, and in not a few others.
such things as I explain in my words.
Such indeed are the wages of your too lofty tongue, Prometheus.
having devised such contrivances, wretched one.
Such then are these things.
